div.head: ECf 32 C
div.ab: De illis, qui possunt et debent de iure cohabitare et remanere in regno Britannie. Britones uero Armorice cum ueniunt in regno isto, suscipi debent et in regno protegi sicut proprii ciues: de corpore regni huius exierunt quondam, de sanguine Britonum regni huius.
div.note: Liebermann’s text transcribed from Gesetze I p. 658 (November 2026): read from the page images and checked against the scan’s own text layer, differences settled against the page.

This passage is not part of ECf or ECf retr: it is one of the additions of the London collection (Leges Anglorum s. XIII in. Londoniis collectae), which Liebermann prints across the page as an insertion into ECf retr. 32 (32 A–E, pp. 655–660). The dictionary cites it as “ECf 32 C …”, so it is kept with ECf here.

note.seg: hier will sich Londoner Fremdenpolitik historisch begründen, mehrfach durch Blutsverwandtschaft, auf welche sich die Engländer damals oft bezogen, wenn Bund mit Deutschen Vortheil versprach; vgl. Math. Paris. 1257, Mon. Germ. 28, 367

here London’s policy towards foreigners seeks a historical foundation, several times through kinship of blood, to which the English then often appealed when alliance with Germans promised advantage; cf. Math. Paris. 1257, Mon. Germ. 28, 367
wohl geschrieben oder veranlasst, bevor 1199 die Personal-Union von England und Bretagne endete, oder als 1207 Herzog Wido Englands Freund war
probably written or occasioned before the personal union of England and Brittany ended in 1199, or when Duke Guy was England’s friend in 1207
sicut homines proprii werden Fremde begünstigt in Freibriefen, so seit 1157 Cölner; Höhlbaum Hansisch. Urk. I S. 8. 16. 22
foreigners are favoured sicut homines proprii in charters, so from 1157 the men of Cologne; Höhlbaum, Hansisch. Urk. I pp. 8. 16. 22
im 5. 6. Jh.; Loth Emigr. Bret. p. 174. Der Londoner benutzt wohl nur Galfr. Monm. XII 15 f.
in the 5th and 6th centuries; Loth, Emigr. Bret. p. 174. The Londoner probably uses only Geoffrey of Monmouth XII 15 f.

div.ab: Concerning those who can and ought by right to live together and remain in the kingdom of Britain. The Britons of Armorica, when they come into this kingdom, ought to be received and protected in the kingdom as its own citizens: they went out once from the body of this kingdom, from the blood of the Britons of this kingdom.

note.seg: Vgl. Gl Bretonen; die Beziehungen Angelsächs. Könige c. 920—31 zu deren Fürsten (EHR 1907, 728) waren dem Verf. sicher unbekannt. Diesem ist vielmehr zuzutrauen, dass er ein Privileg erfunden habe — sogar vielleicht ohne Rücksicht auf gegenwärtige Wirklichkeit — aus blosser pedantischer Spielerei mit Altertümelei und Namensähnlichkeit, die ja sicher in den beiden folgenden Sätzen mindestens für die Begründung des Rechtes der Fremden rein phantastisch mitwirkt. Letzteres aber entsprach um 1200 der Wirklichkeit, und dies Rheinisch-Welfische Vorrecht will Verf. historisch und staatsrechtlich erklären. S. Gl London 32ff.

Cf. Gl Bretonen; the relations of Anglo-Saxon kings c. 920—31 with their princes (EHR 1907, 728) were certainly unknown to the author. He is rather to be credited with having invented a privilege — perhaps even without regard to present reality — out of mere pedantic playing with antiquarianism and similarity of names, which certainly plays a purely fantastic part in the two following sentences at least in the justification of the right of the foreigners. The latter, however, corresponded to reality about 1200, and the author wants to explain this Rhenish-Welf privilege historically and constitutionally. See Gl London 32ff.
